target.title: Development of sEMG sensors and algorithms for silent speech recognition

read.pdf: Figs. 1–6 and Tables 1–2 read, including captions and table rows

entries.text: The authors present face- and neck-worn sensors intended to recognize silently mouthed words and phrases from sEMG.
entries.condition: System description in the abstract; face and neck articulator muscle signals are the input.

entries.text: The authors describe a staged algorithm-development strategy from isolated words, through grammar-constrained sequences, to phoneme models for untrained words.
entries.condition: Authors' stated novelty and experimental development sequence.

entries.text: The final system achieved 8.9% WER and 91.1% recognition rate.
entries.condition: Corpus 3 final triphone system; 1,200 continuous phrases from a 2,200-word vocabulary; results averaged over four task datasets and five subjects listed in Table 2; subject-dependent configuration; features and decoding include MFCC, NL Equivalence Grammar, MLLR, HLDA and SGMM. The paper does not specify a held-out phrase split, random seeds or independent-speaker test.
entries.quote: achieved an 8.9%-word error rate (91.1% recognition rate), far surpassing previous attempts in the field.

entries.text: The lowest individual mean WER in Table 2 was 1.4% for Subject 1.
entries.condition: Subject 1, final system, averaged over digits, text messages, special operations and common phrases in Corpus 3; five subjects appear in the table.

entries.text: The authors characterize their headline score as far surpassing previous attempts.
entries.condition: Authors' comparative claim in the abstract; comparisons are not described as matched evaluations.
entries.quote: far surpassing previous attempts in the field.

entries.text: The authors claim their system's accuracy and vocabulary breadth exceed those in pertinent prior studies.
entries.condition: Discussion comparison with prior studies that use different vocabularies and vocalization conditions.

entries.text: The authors claim that prior work had not combined relevant advances into a portable prototype they considered viable outside controlled laboratory testing.
entries.condition: Discussion claim about the combined prototype; it is not evidence of an outside-laboratory deployment trial.

entries.text: The phoneme-based system is intended to recognize words not used during model training, reducing the need to train on every target word.
entries.condition: The authors' stated aim for Corpus 3; training remains subject-dependent according to the Discussion.
entries.quote: The ability to recognize unseen words is necessary for learning new vocabularies without burdening the users with arduous hours-long training sessions.

entries.text: The study enrolled 19 subjects: 11 female and 8 male, ages 20–42 years, mean age 27.5 years.
entries.unit: subjects; female subjects; male subjects; years; years mean age
entries.condition: Total participants across the experiments before the stated exclusion of three non-compliant participants.

entries.text: Participants were native American English speakers and had no known speech or hearing disabilities.
entries.condition: Study population; no clinical cohort with speech impairment was evaluated in these experiments.

entries.text: Three participants were excluded after review found non-compliance involving noisy or weak sEMG data.
entries.condition: Exclusion was based on intermittent signal noise or signal amplitudes that failed to exceed noise; the paper does not reconcile the total cohort counts with the final table count.
entries.quote: Three participants were non-compliant in this regard and were excluded from the study.

entries.text: The DE 2.1 sEMG acquisition is described as differential, low-noise, band-filtered and 16-bit; its stated sampling rate is 20 kHz.
entries.condition: Acquisition specification stated for the sensor/amplifier setup; Corpus 1 and 2 used tethered DE 2.1 sensors. Trigno Mini sampling is reported separately.

entries.text: Eleven sEMG sensors were fixed to the skin surface.
entries.condition: Sensors were placed over muscles involved in speech production; Table 1 gives anatomical positions and target muscles.
entries.quote: A total of 11 sEMG sensors were fixed to the skin surface.

entries.text: Seven sensors were placed on the neck and chin and four on the face.
entries.condition: The neck/chin placements are sensors 1–7 (submental); face placements are sensors 8–11, as detailed in Table 1.
entries.quote: 7 sensors were placed on the neck and chin (#1–7 submental) and 4 sensors were placed on the face (#8–11)

entries.text: Trigno Mini sensors sampled at 1,926 Hz; DE 2.1 recordings used a Bagnoli amplifier.
entries.condition: Prototype wireless Trigno Mini sensors were used for Corpus 3; tethered DE 2.1 sensors were used for Corpus 1 and 2.

entries.text: Table 1 lists each sensor's anatomical placement and associated target muscles.
entries.condition: Sensor array across submental, ventral neck and facial sites.

entries.text: Each experimental session lasted approximately 4–6 hours, with breaks between recordings.
entries.condition: Across the speech experiments; breaks were intended to reduce fatigue.

entries.text: Subjects recited words shown on a computer monitor, vocally or subvocally; these prompts provide the apparent intended utterances, but the paper does not detail label verification.
entries.condition: Speech prompts were presented in randomized order from one of three language datasets; acoustic signals were also recorded.

entries.text: Corpus 1 included nine subjects and 65 isolated words, including numbers zero through ten and common nouns and verbs.
entries.condition: Corpus 1 isolated-word task; per-subject recordings included vocalized and silently mouthed modes.

entries.text: Each Corpus 1 word was produced three times in pseudo-randomized order in both vocalized and silently mouthed modes.
entries.unit: repetitions per word per speaking mode
entries.condition: Each subject produced the full isolated-word set in both modes; each mode had three instances per word.

entries.text: For Corpus 1, two of three instances per word and speaking mode trained each speaker-specific HMM; the remaining instance was tested.
entries.unit: instances per word and speaking mode
entries.condition: Explicit within-speaker split for the 65-word Corpus 1 experiment; separate models were trained and tested for each speaker.
entries.loc: Methods, Extracting features for recognizing isolated words

entries.text: Corpus 2 comprised 1,200 word sequences from a 202-word vocabulary, with mean phrase length of 6.0 words, for four subjects.
entries.unit: subjects; sequences; vocabulary words; mean words per phrase
entries.condition: Corpus 2 small-vocabulary continuous sequence task; all subjects recited in subvocal mode; partition and speaker overlap are not reported.

entries.text: Corpus 3 comprised nearly 1,200 phrases, mean 6.4 words per phrase, drawn from a 2,200-word vocabulary, for six subjects.
entries.unit: subjects; phrases; mean words per phrase; vocabulary words
entries.condition: Corpus 3 large-vocabulary continuous subvocal task. Table 2 reports five subjects; the relation between the six described here and five tabulated subjects is not explained.
entries.quote: In total, 6 subjects were presented with nearly 1200 phrases (mean words/phrase = 6.4) generated from a 2200-word vocabulary

entries.text: The authors implemented real-time finite-state speech activity detection during sEMG acquisition.
entries.condition: Detection identifies speech-related start and end points in sEMG rather than relying on post-collection processing.

entries.text: The detector used 40 ms envelope windows with 20 ms overlap and adapted to background activity and speaker/utterance maximum energy.
entries.condition: Online local per-channel thresholding followed by global activity decision across channels.

entries.text: The isolated-word MFCC representation used six coefficients over 0–2.5 kHz, with 50 ms windows and a 25 ms frame rate.
entries.condition: MFCC features computed from sEMG for Corpus 1; eleven channels supplied the overall sensor data. Frame parameters are recorded in t75.
entries.loc: Methods, Extracting features for recognizing isolated words

entries.text: The isolated-word HMMs had ten left-to-right states, eight emitting and two degenerate, with a single Gaussian per parameter.
entries.unit: states; emitting states; degenerate states; Gaussian distribution per parameter
entries.condition: HTK isolated-word models for Corpus 1; separate speaker and speaking-mode models; training/test split is recorded in t21.
entries.loc: Methods, Extracting features for recognizing isolated words

entries.text: MFCCs yielded the lowest average WER, 9.6%, across the tested feature combinations.
entries.condition: Corpus 1, 65 isolated words; nine subjects; per-speaker and per-speaking-mode HMMs; two of three token instances trained and one tested; 10-state single-Gaussian HMM. Figure 2 averages feature-combination comparisons.

entries.text: The sEMG coactivation index had 41.2% WER, nearly four times the MFCC errors.
entries.condition: Same Corpus 1 feature-combination comparison and speaker/mode split as t28.

entries.text: Four grammar models were compared: sentence-construction, unrestricted NATO, NL equivalence and unigram grammar.
entries.condition: HTK word-sequence recognition using MFCCs, ten HMM states and two Gaussian mixtures per state; Corpus 2, 202-word vocabulary. The evaluation split is not specified.
entries.loc: Methods, Modeling grammatical context to recognize sequences of words

entries.text: Sentence-construction grammar achieved the lowest reported WER, 5.8%.
entries.condition: Corpus 2 grammar comparison; 1,200 sequences, 202-word vocabulary, four subjects; MFCC word HMM with ten states and two mixtures/state; paper does not specify the test partition, seed or validation data.
entries.quote: The lowest WER of 5.8% was achieved using the grammar model that was based on the sentence-construction rules used to generate the 1200-sentence corpus.

entries.text: NL Equivalence Grammar achieved 6.8% WER, the second-lowest result among the tested grammar models.
entries.condition: Same Corpus 2 grammar comparison as t31; 1,200 sequences and 202-word vocabulary across four subjects; split and validation protocol are not specified.
entries.quote: provides a comparable WER of 6.8% (the second lowest in amongst the models tested)

entries.text: The authors say the best-scoring sentence-construction grammar is an upper bound because it is the most restrictive and tailored to the tested corpus.
entries.condition: Corpus 2 grammar comparison; the authors instead chose the more general NL Equivalence Grammar for subsequent tests.
entries.quote: While this grammar model provides an upper bound on recognition performance it is also the most restrictive

entries.text: The phoneme system used five-state left-to-right HMMs for 37 phonemes covered by Corpus 2.
entries.condition: HTK phoneme models; tested on Corpus 2 sequences from the 202-word vocabulary; partition and speaker overlap are not reported.
entries.loc: Methods, Phoneme recognition of unseen continuous speech

entries.text: Increasing mixtures per phoneme-HMM state from four to eight reduced average WER from about 24% to about 15%.
entries.unit: Gaussian mixtures per state; % average WER
entries.condition: Corpus 2, 202-word word-sequence task; four subjects; five-state phoneme HMMs; test partition and selection data are not specified.
entries.quote: increasing the number of Gaussian mixtures per state from 4 to 8 significantly reduced the average WER from approximately 24% to about 15%.
entries.loc: Results, Phoneme recognition of continuous speech; Fig. 4

entries.text: Sixteen Gaussian mixtures per HMM state gave the reported optimum average WER of 11.3%.
entries.unit: Gaussian mixtures per state; % average WER
entries.condition: Corpus 2, 202-word sequences across four subjects; five-state phoneme HMMs; split, seed and independent validation are not reported.
entries.loc: Results, Phoneme recognition of continuous speech; Fig. 4

entries.text: HLDA reduced features to approximately 40 dimensions and reduced average WER from 11.3% to 7.3%.
entries.condition: Corpus 2 phoneme recognition task with 202-word vocabulary and four subjects; model uses 16 mixtures/state; evaluation split and data used to select dimensions are not reported.
entries.quote: reducing the number of feature dimensions to approximately 40 using HLDA reduced the average WER from 11.3% to 7.3%.

entries.text: The combined Corpus 3 representation used 112 features and a single full-covariance Gaussian model had over 10,000 parameters.
entries.condition: Motivation for MLLR and SGMM to compact the model and improve results with smaller amounts of training data.

entries.text: The exhaustive subset evaluation covered 2,047 possible subsets of the 11-sensor array.
entries.condition: Sensor-subset search evaluated speaker-dependent WER averaged across speakers at each subset cardinality; the paper does not state a separate validation/test split for choosing the best subset.
entries.quote: we conducted an exhaustive evaluation of the full array of 11 sensors, of which there are 11-choose-k subsets of size k, totaling 2047 possible subsets.

questions.q: How strongly does the headline score establish recognition of genuinely unseen phrases and independent speakers?
questions.answer: The authors report the final score on Corpus 3 and describe recognition of words unseen during training, but do not provide a separate held-out phrase protocol or speaker-independent evaluation. The model is explicitly subject-dependent, and the Corpus 3 methods count differs from the number of subjects tabulated. The evidence supports the reported task-specific result, while the generalization boundary remains unclear.

questions.q: What limits the paper's claim of practical readiness?
questions.answer: The authors acknowledge that longer-duration sensor testing is still needed and that the subject-dependent system requires separate user training. They also say the available sEMG data are too limited for a representative subject-independent model; proposed adaptation to reduce training time is future work rather than an evaluated result.

questions.q: Are the comparisons with earlier WER results controlled head-to-head comparisons?
questions.answer: No matched comparison protocol is described. The cited results differ in vocabulary size, speaking mode, speaker population and task; one comparator used vocalized speech. Treat the superiority statement as the authors' cross-study comparison, not a controlled comparative experiment.
